cue.topic: Describe a film that made a strong impression on you
bullets: what the film was called and what it was about
when and where you watched it
and explain why it made such a strong impression on you

part2.model: I'd like to talk about an animated film called Coco, which I watched about three years ago and still think about today. It follows a young Mexican boy named Miguel, who dreams of becoming a musician even though his family has banned music for generations. One night he ends up in the Land of the Dead, where he uncovers the truth about his great-great-grandfather. I watched it at a small neighbourhood cinema with my younger cousin, Farah. To be honest, I only agreed to go because she begged me, and I expected a lighthearted cartoon. I was completely wrong. About halfway through, the story took a turn I did not see coming, and by the end I was fighting back tears, while Farah was sobbing quietly beside me. What struck me most was the way the film deals with memory and family. The idea that people live on as long as someone remembers them really stayed with me. The music was stunning as well, and the vibrant colours made every scene a feast for the eyes. Afterwards, Farah and I sat in the car park for ages, talking about our grandparents. It reminded me how precious those relationships are, so I phoned my grandmother that very evening. Looking back, it was more than just entertainment. It was a gentle push to cherish the people I love, and that is why it made such a lasting impression.

I suspect cinemas will survive by offering something special, such as immersive screens and live events. In other words, they will move upmarket rather than vanish.

questions.q: Do you think entertainment should aim to educate as well as amuse?

However, the most memorable stories often teach us something without feeling like a lecture. Historical dramas, for example, can bring the past to life in a way textbooks rarely manage. I think the best producers strike a balance, offering a gripping plot while quietly broadening the audience's outlook. If viewers learn something by accident, that is a bonus.

questions.q: Should governments control violent content in films and video games?
questions.model: I believe some regulation is necessary, particularly to protect young children. Age ratings already help parents decide what is suitable, but they are often ignored online. Repeated exposure to graphic violence may make aggression seem normal, so parents also need to talk openly with their children about what they watch. However, I wouldn't want governments to go too far, since heavy-handed censorship can restrict creative freedom. A sensible compromise is clear labelling combined with strict enforcement on platforms aimed at minors.
